claims.statement: Misleading details given by another person after an event (a co-witness's account, their statements) change what people later report remembering of it.
claims.exposure: misleading details from another person after the event (a co-witness's account or statements)
claims.comparison: consistent information, or none, after the event
claims.outcome: accuracy of later reports of the event's details

claims.statement: Repeated suggestion can lead some people to remember, as their own, a whole childhood event that never happened.
claims.exposure: repeated suggestion of a false childhood event (a relative's account, interviews, imagining it)
claims.comparison: true childhood events, or no suggestion
claims.outcome: reporting a memory of the false event

claims.statement: Even the memories we feel sure of are often wrong: feeling certain says little about being right.
So we should trust our own memory and certainty less: doubting one's memory protects against being wrong or misled.
claims.exposure: distrusting one's own memory (the book's advice, « trust yourself less »)
claims.outcome: accuracy of what one reports; being misled less

notFound: no published meta-analysis of the misinformation effect itself: the only one (Edmar, Enquist & Luke, 480 studies) is a PsyArXiv preprint (10.31234/osf.io/m68kf_v6, v6 of 2026-10-01, no published version), refused by the verifier
no preregistered multi-lab replication of the misinformation effect or of implantation done before data collection: Ito et al. 2019 registered its second wave formally only after collection
no published meta-analysis of memory conformity between co-witnesses

no sample from an Arab country on misinformation, implantation or confidence, except one weak, unread Saudi study (Hassan et al. 2018, 10.30958/ajl.4-4-3, not kept); Egypt only in a lineup study on headscarves (Megreya et al. 2011), off topic

no study of confidence and accuracy for everyday memories of conversations (who said what, who was to do what); the only evidence on one's own life is about memories of shocking news (Talarico 2003; Hirst 2015, not kept: an attack)
no direct comparison of the misinformation effect in the lab and in real events; one case study of a real robbery (Odinot 2009, 14 witnesses) not kept
Sporer et al. 1995 (confidence-accuracy meta-analysis) and Yuille & Cutshall 1986: no abstract anywhere, not kept
Wiechert 2026: full text closed and no preprint found: sample size and country unknown

Dalton & Daneman 2006 (10.1080/09658210500495073): its central-vs-peripheral result sentence is read by the verifier's role cues as a method sentence (« participants were »): not kept; Bilgin & Wang 2024 carries the point
Manson's book not read (no copy): ch. 6 located by two readers' Kindle highlights; his 2016 article read in full

found.note: against « rewritten »: with a particular procedure (two answers possible, detail and source asked apart) the misinformation effect was undone, even 5 weeks later: the original detail was still there. Same author as Blank 2014
McCloskey & Zaragoza 1985: with a modified test, misleading information left memory of the original event intact; old and debated, Oeberst 2012 carries the point: no « memory erased » in any line
Edmar et al. 2026, preprint meta-analysis (480 studies, g = 0.69, CI 0.26-1.13, I² 92%): robust but partly strategic and very variable; refused by the verifier, evidence page only

against « easily »: less influence for central than for peripheral details; who should send the file (or which day) is central for the colleagues, so expect less than Ito's details (Dalton 2006 says the same, sheet dropped)
Odinot et al. 2009, 14 witnesses of a real robbery: 84% correct, a TV reconstruction did not alter memories, confidence-accuracy r = 0.38; one case, not kept
full text: details adopted in 626 of 708 undisputed cases, 1 of 58 disputed (unplanned): the scene has no dispute; card says « تفصيلة », not « رواية »; no collectivist pattern across countries

against c2's figure, not its direction: the same Murphy data give 35% or 4% depending on coding; participants credit themselves with fewer false memories than coders. Debate open in 2025 (Wade et al., Brewin & Andrews): no figure on screen
Wade, Garry & Pezdek 2018: coding makes the rate (70% to 26-30%), on false memories of a crime: same point as Andrews, outside the episode's register
Otgaar et al. 2022: online implantation without interviewer, 9-30%; rates drop with more people and less interaction (Gewehr 2026 preprint: 8.5%): « some », never a rate

the key piece for c3: both camps agree confidence tells about accuracy « varies predictably »; « certainty says little » is the old view they leave. Narrative, low rank: an agreement, not one more proof

for the book on c3: the only evidence on one's own life; for shocking news, belief in accuracy stayed while agreement with one's first account fell. Small (54), not transposed to a happy or everyday memory
Hirst et al. 2015, 10-year follow-up: confidence stayed high despite forgetting; supports c3 but about an attack: evidence page only, never in a scene
Eisen & Ying 2026: confidence and accuracy correlate, yet nearly half of false identifications made at 90-100% confidence under suggestive procedures: limits « a first certainty is mostly right »

Giacona et al. 2021 and Moore et al. 2025 (10.1186/s41235-025-00692-9): viewing conditions can compromise even high-confidence identifications: hence « has weight, but is no proof », never « غالبًا صح »

Bird et al. 2024: neither the Self-Administered Interview nor written free recall reduced susceptibility (Chan 2017 also against): the note is a trace to go back to, never « so your memory does not change »

Vredeveldt et al. 2018, 86 police officers: recording one's own memories before collaborating left fewer errors in the joint report; Horry 2020 meta-analysis (10.1002/acp.3753) backs an early written account: the takeaway, as « جرّب »

Dudek & Polczyk 2023, registered report: induced memory distrust did not change suggestibility as predicted; van Bergen 2009 and Torrance 2025 point to a cost: c4 out of scope, never « ما تثقش في ذاكرتك »
Hassan et al. 2018, the only Arab sample found (Saudi law students): weak journal, size unknown, full text unread; would not lift the applicability line. Megreya 2011 (Egypt) is off topic

counterEvidence.conclusion: ⚖️ holds; ❌ cannot be argued; ✅ only on a narrower reading of c3, refused. Taken: certainty low (c3 indirect and mixed), « reported », never « rewritten », c2 « some » with no figure, the scene without dispute, Ito kept on screen with « تفصيلة », the note as a trace to go back to. Not taken: c1 lowered for applicability (10 countries, two cultural groups).
